outcome: The only substantive advance on this conjecture — that large stable fields are separably closed, a case obtained by restricting to 'large' fields — was proved by Johnson, Tran, Walsberg and Ye in a preprint posted 4 September 2020 (arXiv:2009.02319), well before the 26 January 2024 frozen revision, and later appeared in the Journal of the European Mathematical Society (online June 2023, print issue 2024). A July 2026 preprint by Kaplan, Matthews and Walsberg ('Building trees in large fields', arXiv:2607.16942) gives a substantially simpler proof of the same case (and of the related fact that large simple fields are bounded) but does not extend the result to any new case and does not touch the general conjecture, so it is not itself a scope-changing event under §3.1. The general stable field conjecture — every infinite field with a stable first-order theory is separably closed — remains open.
summary: The stable field conjecture (every infinite stable field is separably closed) is a long-standing open problem in model theory, with partial progress predating the window: Scanlon (1999) showed infinite stable fields are Artin-Schreier closed, and Johnson, Tran, Walsberg and Ye (arXiv:2009.02319, posted 2020-09-04, published in JEMS with online publication 2023-06-15 and a 2024 print issue) proved the case of 'large' stable fields, via a new étale-open topology. Both the decisive preprint and its journal appearance (dated by first written argument, per §6.3, not by journal print date) predate or straddle the 26 January 2024 freeze in a way that keeps the underlying mathematical event pre-window, so this is classified open_stale rather than a fresh partial result. Within the window, the only new item found is arXiv:2607.16942 ('Building trees in large fields', Kaplan, Matthews, Walsberg, posted 2026-07-18), which gives a substantially simplified, more conceptual proof of the same 'large stable fields are separably closed' result (and a companion result on large simple fields being bounded) using an explicit tree-building technique. I read the full abstract/HTML of this paper and found no claim of a new case, no extension of the boundary of what's known, and no mention of AI or machine-learning tools in the research. Because it re-derives an already-known case rather than restricting the conjecture's scope further, it does not constitute a new event under §3.1's case-vs-variant test — it is a proof simplification, not new mathematical territory. The general conjecture (for arbitrary infinite stable fields, not just 'large' ones) remains fully open, and I found no work in the window addressing it directly. I also checked arXiv:2508.10886 ('Large implies henselian', Johnson-Tran-Walsberg-Ye, 2025-08-14) which is about characterizing large fields via henselianity and does not mention the stable field conjecture at all. No AI involvement was found anywhere in this research area.
competing_reading: One could argue the JEMS publication (online 2023-06-15, print 2024) should count as the dating event since journal acceptance is when the result becomes 'digested by experts' (resolved-tier evidence), and since the print issue is dated 2024, arguably later than the frozen revision's January 2024 timestamp. But §6.3 is explicit that journal publication date should never be used for dating since it lags the real event and would spuriously pull pre-window results into the window; the first written argument (the 2020 preprint) is what governs, and it was already digested (via peer review) well before 2024 regardless. I am confident in open_stale here.
what_would_settle_it: A proof (or disproof) of the conjecture for the general (not necessarily large) infinite stable field case would resolve or refute the conjecture outright; a paper explicitly extending 'large' to some broader class would count as further partial progress and change the status to partial with a new dated event.
